Issued at 235 PM CDT Fri Aug 7 2026

A subtle shortwave trough is progressing across the Upper 
Midwest with a cold front lagging behind the wave and stretching
from central MN to eastern NE. Ahead of the front, a complex of
thunderstorms has developed in southern MN and northern IA 
which has started to turn towards the south as of recent radar 
trends. The expectation is for this thunderstorm complex to 
continue to dive southward across eastern IA this evening and 
gradually weaken as it does so. Therefore, dry conditions should
prevail locally with partly cloudy skies and temperatures in 
the mid-80s this afternoon cooling into the upper 60s to around 
70 overnight. However, with only modest capping being noted in 
recent amdar soundings and the 18z DVN Raob; there is a low 
chance that a few scattered showers or storms could drift into 
northwest IL later this evening. If this was to occur, the main 
concern with any showers/storms would be lightning and locally 
heavy downpours but some locally gusty winds cannot be fully 
ruled out. For now have opted to maintain a 20-30% chance for 
showers and thunderstorms through our forecast area tonight as a
precaution. 

By daybreak Saturday morning, any showers/storms that survive 
into our area should be eroded leaving us with another tranquil 
and seasonably warm summer day. Winds though will be out of the 
northwest behind the aforementioned front, but temperatures are 
still expected to top out in the mid-80s Saturday afternoon. 
Otherwise, expect mostly sunny skies through Saturday evening. 

Heading into Saturday night, a building ridge of over the 
southwest CONUS will help to deepen a broad trough over the 
Upper Midwest and northern Great Lakes. This will in turn 
generate stout northwest flow over northern IL and northwest IN 
and allow several shortwaves to dive through the region Saturday
night through at least the middle of next week. The first of 
these shortwaves is forecast to move through the region Saturday
night into Sunday and lead to the development of a complex of 
thunderstorms somewhere near the SD/MN border. Given that the 
highest instability axis should be stretching from eastern IA 
southeastward into central IL, this complex should traverse 
somewhere near or west of this axis Saturday night and thus keep
the bulk of any storms west of us. However, if this axis is 
able to shift east then the storm complex could brush our 
western counties late Saturday night into Sunday morning. The 
favored scenario right now is that the storms stay west of our 
area Saturday night, but have opted to keep some 30-40% POPs in 
the forecast for our western half to account for some lingering 
uncertainty in the exact storm track. 

Regardless on how Saturday night goes, a warm front is expected
to lift into northern IL and northwest IN on Sunday which will 
surge a warm, humid, and unstable air mass into the area. Couple
this with the lingering ascent associated with the shortwave 
aloft and conditions look to be favorable for additional 
thunderstorms to develop Sunday afternoon and persist into the 
evening. While guidance is in good agreement on thunderstorms 
occurring Sunday, there continues to be some uncertainty in 
storm coverage and the exact timeframe storms will occur. That 
said, with the large amount of instability (3000-6000 J/kg) and 
40-45 kts of deep layer shear any storms that develop on Sunday 
could become severe and contain a threat for damaging winds, 
hail, and maybe even a threat for tornadoes. With the 
aforementioned uncertainties the latest Day 3 outlook from SPC 
does have our area in a marginal (level 1 of 5) risk for this 
potential. 

An additional period of thunderstorms are forecast for Monday 
as another shortwave pivots across the region. Similar to 
Sunday, the environment will be warm, humid, and unstable which 
will support a fair coverage of thunderstorms especially during 
the afternoon and evening hours. However, confidence on coverage
and the exact timing of storms is low and will likely depend on
how storms evolve on Sunday. Nevertheless, any storms that 
materialize on Monday will also have a chance to become severe 
and thus SPC has put our area in the 15% (slight risk) outlook 
for Monday. 

Beyond Monday the forecast through the middle of next week 
looks to favor more periods of showers and thunderstorms as 
shortwaves continue to round the trough overhead. While there is
a chance that as repeated rounds of storms occur that the 
outflows from storms push the better storm environment south of 
the area and give us a break, confidence on when or if this will
occur remains low. So for now our official forecast will keep 
40-60% chances for storms around through much of next week, but 
suspect changes to these will occur as trends present 
themselves. Otherwise, expect seasonably warm temperatures to 
prevail with highs in the 80s and overnight lows in the 60s.

Yack
